source.title: Projection Algorithms: Results and Open Problems

accepted.question_text: Let X be a real Hilbert space and let C = C1 ∩ ··· ∩ CN be a nonempty intersection of closed convex sets. Bregman's result states that the sequence generated by cyclic projections converges weakly to some point of C. Must this convergence always be strong (that is, convergence in norm), or can there exist examples in which cyclic projections converge only weakly and not in norm?
accepted.context_brief: weak vs norm convergence for cyclic projections

evidence.quote: Fact 2.3 (Bregman). [17] If C 6= ;, then the sequence of cyclic projections converges weakly to some point in C.
Open Problem 1. In Bregman's result (Fact 2.3), can the convergence be only weak?

accepted.question_text: In the specific setting X = ℓ² where C1 is the cone of nonnegative sequences and C2 is a hyperplane with nonempty intersection C = C1 ∩ C2, Fact 3.4 proves that alternating projections always converge in norm. What happens if the hyperplane C2 is replaced by an affine subspace of finite codimension? In particular, does the same norm-convergence phenomenon still hold in that finite-codimensional affine-subspace setting?

evidence.quote: Fact 3.4. [8, Theorem 5.3.(iv)] In X := `2, let C1 be the cone of nonnegative sequences and C2 be an arbitrary hyperplane with C = C1 \cap C2 6= ;. Then the sequence of alternating projections always converges in norm.
Open Problem 2. What happens in Fact 3.4 if replace C2 by an affine subspace of finite codimension?

accepted.question_text: For cyclic projections onto three or more closed convex sets whose intersection is empty, what is the asymptotic behavior of the projection sequence? More specifically, is there an analogue for the N-set inconsistent case of the two-set dichotomy described in Fact 4.1, including an appropriate replacement for the displacement vector v that governs the behavior of alternating projections for two sets?
accepted.context_brief: inconsistent cyclic projections for three or more sets

evidence.quote: Open Problem 3. What is the behavior of the sequence of cyclic projections for three or more sets with empty intersection?

The crux of the problem is this: the vector v in Fact 4.1 is well-defined and important for the formulation of the behavior of the sequence of alternating projections even when the distance d(C1; C2) = inf{||c1 - c2|| : c1 in C1; c2 in C2} is not attained, i.e., v 62 C2 - C1; however, it is not known how to define the vector(s) analogous to v in the N-set case.

accepted.question_text: Suppose each Ci is a subspace of a real Hilbert space, C = C1 ∩ ··· ∩ CN is nonempty, and z_{n+1} = P_{r(n+1)} z_n is the sequence generated by a random map r that hits every index in {1, ..., N} infinitely often. Fact 5.1 shows that this random-projection sequence converges weakly to a point of C. Must such convergence in the subspace case always improve to norm convergence, or can random projections onto subspaces converge only weakly?

evidence.quote: Fact 5.1 (Amemiya and Ando). [1] Suppose each Ci is a subspace. Then the sequence of random projections converges weakly to a point in C.
Open Problem 4. In Fact 5.1, can the convergence be only weak?

accepted.question_text: Let C = C1 ∩ ··· ∩ CN be a nonempty intersection of closed convex sets in a real Hilbert space, and let z_{n+1} = P_{r(n+1)} z_n be the sequence of random projections determined by a random map r that visits every set infinitely often. Does this sequence always converge weakly to some point of C for general closed convex sets, beyond the special subspace case covered by Fact 5.1?
accepted.context_brief: random projections for general closed convex sets

evidence.quote: In this section, we assume that C = \cap_{i=1}^N Ci 6= ; ... and r : {1, 2, ...} ! {1, 2, ..., N} is a random map, i.e., it is onto and assumes every value infinitely often. We are interested in the method of random projections, i.e., the behavior of the sequence (zn) defined by z0 in X; z_{n+1} := P_{r(n+1)} z_n, for all n >= 0.
Open Problem 5. Does the sequence of random projections converge weakly to some point in C?

accepted.question_text: Assume each Ci is a subspace, let T = P_N P_{N-1} ··· P_1, and define an acceleration scheme A by A(x) = (1 - t_x)x + t_x T x, where t_x is chosen so that ||A(x)|| is minimal. Starting from z0 in X, set z_n = A^{n-1}(T z0) for n >= 1. Fact 6.1 states that (z_n) always converges weakly to P_C z0, converges in norm when N = 2, and converges linearly when {C1, ..., CN} is boundedly linearly regular. Can (z_n) fail to converge in norm when N >= 3, or when the family {C1, ..., CN} is not boundedly linearly regular?
accepted.context_brief: acceleration scheme beyond N=2 or regular case

evidence.quote: Fact 6.1. [15,14] (i) (zn) always converges weakly to P_C z0. (ii) (zn) converges in norm, if N = 2. (iii) (zn) converges linearly, if {C1, ..., CN} is boundedly linearly regular.
Open Problem 6. Can (zn) fail to converge in norm when N >= 3 or when {C1, ..., CN} is not boundedly linearly regular?

trace.notes: Resolved the zbMATH record to the author-hosted PostScript full text and identified the title page plus the sections containing Open Problems 1-6.
Extracted Open Problem 1 from the section discussing Bregman's cyclic-projection theorem.
Extracted Open Problem 2 from the discussion immediately following Fact 3.4.
Extracted Open Problem 3 from the inconsistent-case section and retained the explanatory sentence about the missing N-set analogue of v.
Extracted Open Problem 4 from the random-projections section for subspaces.
Extracted Open Problem 5 from the random-projections section for general closed convex sets.
Extracted Open Problem 6 from the acceleration section.
Expanded the question so the Hilbert-space setting, the cyclic-projection setting, and the weak-vs-strong distinction are explicit in the question text.
Expanded Fact 3.4 into a self-contained finite-codimension variant question.
Made explicit that the open issue concerns three or more sets with empty intersection and the absence of an N-set analogue of the displacement vector v.
Restated the random-map setup and the subspace hypothesis so the question is self-contained.
Restated the random-projection iteration and generalized the question from subspaces to arbitrary closed convex sets using only source-supported context.
Inlined the acceleration map A, the sequence definition, and the known convergence guarantees from Fact 6.1.
No near-duplicate open problems were merged; the six extracted questions are distinct.
All accepted items include verbatim evidence with page locators and were rewritten to avoid dangling references to facts or sections.
